sink: spawn(shellConfig.command, [...shellConfig.args, args.command], {cwd, stdio:[...]}) at src/index.ts:577-581 passes args.command as a single argv element to bash.exe -c / cmd.exe /c / powershell.exe -Command, which each then parse it as a full script/command line

A command string containing an embedded newline, e.g. "echo hi\nrm -rf /", contains none of the blocked operator characters and parses (via parseCommand) as command='echo', args=['hi\nrm','-rf','/'] -- neither 'rm' (a default-blocked command) nor the chained statement is ever inspected. When this single string is handed to bash -c (gitbash shell) or powershell -Command, the shell's own grammar treats a raw newline exactly like ';' -- a statement separator -- so the blocked 'rm -rf /' executes anyway.
why: Verified directly: validation.ts's blockedOperators-derived regex never includes \n or \r, and parseCommand/isCommandBlocked/isArgumentBlocked only ever look at the first whitespace-delimited token, never at content after an embedded newline. config.ts:26 confirms restrictWorkingDirectory/enableInjectionProtection/blockedCommands are all enabled by default, so this is a live bypass of the tool's own advertised, on-by-default security feature (blocking dangerous commands like rm/del/format/shutdown/reg/net and chaining operators), not merely the tool executing what it's told -- the whole point of blockedCommands+blockedOperators is defeated by a single embedded newline. (Separately and additionally, execute_command's restrictWorkingDirectory check at src/index.ts:560-562 uses workingDir.startsWith(allowedPath) with no path-separator boundary, so a workingDir like '<home>-evil' also bypasses the directory restriction against the default allowedPaths=[os.homedir(), process.cwd()] -- a second, independent guard-bypass on the same tool.)
